title: Public but Not Enforceable: Canada's ELD 1.3.1 and the Living Certified List
summary: CCMTA ELD 1.3.1 is public but not in force. Match device IDs to Transport Canada's list, plan provider upgrades, and set revocation cover holds.
body_markdown:
A broker covers a dry van out of Mississauga for a Monday morning delivery in Windsor. The carrier's power unit has run the same ELD for three years. The device still boots, still syncs, still looks fine on the dash. On Friday afternoon, an inspector at a scale house checks Transport Canada's list of certified electronic logging devices and finds the identifier marked revoked as of October 13, 2026. The truck is federally regulated. The device is no longer on the list the carrier is required to use. The load is late before anyone updates the ETA.


That is one track of Canada's ELD problem in late 2026. The other is quieter. On July 29, 2026, Transport Canada made public CCMTA's Technical Standard for Electronic Logging Devices version 1.3.1, dated July 22, 2026. It replaces version 1.3, which had been posted September 29, 2025. The text is available. The coming-into-force date is not. Transport Canada says it will lead implementation, that providers and certification bodies will need a transition period, and that more guidance on testing, certification and roadside enforcement will follow. As of early November 2026, no effective date has been published.


Canadian federally regulated carriers, and brokers covering Canadian capacity, now run two clocks at once. One is a national technical standard that is public but not yet enforceable. The other is a live certified-device list that can revoke mid-operation. Neither is the U.S. FMCSA registry story. Canada's list and process are separate, and treating them as interchangeable is how cross-border fleets get surprised at the border.


## What 1.3.1 actually changes (and what it does not)


CCMTA's summary of amendments frames most of 1.3.1 as clarification of definitions and device behaviour, not a rewrite of the federal hours-of-service rule. The themes it covers include ELD events, geo-location, engine hours, unidentified driving, manual entries, edits and annotations, data transfer, malfunction self-monitoring and hours-of-service limits.


That matters for planning. Your provider may need a software update, a recertification, or both once Transport Canada sets the transition clock. Until then, devices certified to the current technical standard version shown on Transport Canada's list remain the ones you can use. Version 1.3.1 sitting on ccmta.ca does not, by itself, invalidate a certified device. Waiting for the government date without asking your provider for a roadmap is also a mistake. Soft transitions still produce hard cutovers for fleets that never booked the upgrade window.


Transport Canada's ELD page is explicit about the process gap: following CCMTA approval, Transport Canada leads implementation and coming into force, recognizing that ELD providers and certification bodies need a period of transition before full implementation of 1.3.1. The same page says it will update with information on testing and certification and on regulatory requirements that apply to roadside enforcement. Until those updates land, treat 1.3.1 as a procurement and vendor-management problem, not a roadside citation yet.


## The certified list is already enforceable


The federal ELD mandate for federally regulated commercial drivers has been in place since June 12, 2021. Transport Canada's guidance for motor carriers and drivers is unambiguous: the device must comply with the Commercial Vehicle Drivers Hours of Service Regulations and the ELD Technical Standard, and it must be listed on Transport Canada's list of certified electronic logging devices. As a motor carrier, you are responsible for making sure the devices your drivers use are certified.


That responsibility does not end at purchase. The list has certified and revoked sections. Status can change after a device has been in your fleet for years. A check of the list on November 6, 2026, still shows the October 13, 2026 revocation of identifier DT4000 (certification number 6T16), a Windows application certified March 24, 2023. A related Android identifier from the same vendor family, DT4R10, still appears as certified. The lesson is not about any single brand. It is that identifiers and certification numbers matter more than product marketing names, and that one SKU in a lineup can drop while another remains active.


Transport Canada's list page also notes that certification bodies maintain overall authority over a model's certification status, and that questions about a specific model go to that body. Revocations in 2026 have not been limited to one month. Entries marked revoked appear across January through October. Searching the list once when you buy a device is not a compliance program.


Unlike some U.S. registry actions that publish an explicit multi-week transition before out-of-service treatment, Transport Canada's carrier pages do not advertise a fixed grace period after a Canadian revocation. Do not invent one. If your identifier shows revoked, treat cover and dispatch as blocked until you have a certified replacement plan, paper-log contingency where still allowed under the regulations, and documentation for roadside.


## US trucks in Canada are a separate checklist


Cross-border fleets often assume an FMCSA-registered device is good enough north of the border. Transport Canada's post-mandate guidance says otherwise. After June 12, 2021, U.S.-based motor carriers and drivers operating under Canada's federal rules must use devices that meet Canada's regulations and technical standard, tested and certified by a certification body accredited by Transport Canada. A device that meets both Canadian and American regulations can work, but Canadian certification is the gate. U.S. exemptions are not recognized in Canada.


That is why brokers covering Canadian capacity cannot rely on a carrier's U.S. ELD screenshot alone. Ask for the Canadian ELD identifier and certification number, then match both to Transport Canada's list before the truck crosses. Asset fleets with mixed U.S. and Canadian power need the same match in the tractor master, not in a shared folder of PDFs.


The brief contrast with the United States is enough: FMCSA's August and October 2026 revocation waves, and the grace-period mechanics that followed them, are a U.S. process. Canada's certified list and CCMTA technical standard run on a different calendar. Syncing only the U.S. registry will miss a Canadian revocation, and vice versa.


## Asset, broker and hybrid: different failure modes


**Asset carriers** feel a revocation as parked power, missed revenue miles and a scramble for certified replacements. They also own the in-cab packet: user's manual, data-transfer instructions, printed malfunction instructions and enough blank records of duty status for at least 15 days, as Transport Canada requires for each commercial vehicle. A 1.3.1 transition that needs hardware swaps or engine-sync retests will hit capital and shop time. Encode device identifier, certification number, certification body and technical standard version on every unit, and refresh that inventory against the federal list on a schedule, not after a citation.


**Brokers** feel it when a covered truck fails at a scale or at the border and the customer still expects the original appointment. The carrier relationship does not transfer the compliance duty away from the operating carrier, but the broker still owns the service failure. Capacity rules that require a current Canadian ELD identifier before cover, and that hold dispatch when an identifier appears on the revoked section, prevent Friday-afternoon surprises. Brokers that only ask "do you have an ELD" are asking the 2019 question.


**Hybrids** get both problems on the same day: a company tractor whose identifier dropped off the list, and a brokered unit that never disclosed a Canadian certification number. One customer-facing compliance policy for Canadian federal work, with explicit exceptions only where provincial-only rules truly apply, keeps the asset and brokerage desks from inventing different answers for the same lane.


Provincial rules still matter at the edges. Transport Canada notes that federal requirements cover federally regulated (extra-provincial) operations, and it maintains links to provincial and territorial governments for drivers who remain inside a single province. Confirm which regime each load sits under before you assume the federal certified list is or is not the controlling check.


## What to do before Transport Canada names a date


Four operating moves close most of the gap without waiting for the coming-into-force notice.


1.


**Inventory by identifier.** Pull ELD identifier and certification number from every tractor that runs Canadian federal work. Match them to Transport Canada's list. Flag revoked and unknown entries the same day.


2.


**Ask providers for a 1.3.1 plan.** Software-only update, recertification, hardware change, and estimated customer window. Get it in writing. If the answer is "we will wait for Transport Canada," ask what waiting means for your fleet's cutover capacity.


3.


**Wire cover and dispatch holds.** Capacity that cannot show a currently certified Canadian identifier does not cover federal Canadian freight. Statuses and permissions should make the hold visible to ops, not bury it in a compliance inbox.


4.


**Keep the roadside packet current.** Malfunction procedures, blank logs and transfer instructions fail inspections even when the device itself is certified. Treat packet audits as part of the same program as list checks.


Every freight business is unique in how it mixes asset and brokerage, Canadian and U.S. power, dedicated and spot. The shops that stay out of scale-house trouble encode that uniqueness into rules, statuses, permissions and capacity logic: which identifiers are allowed on which lanes, who can override a hold, who gets notified when a certification status flips, and how billing and visibility change when a truck is pulled for equipment. A policy memo that nobody's workflow reads will not survive the next revocation batch.


## The decision, not the PDF


Version 1.3.1 is already public. The certified list is already moving. The decision for Canadian federal work in November 2026 is not whether to read the standard. It is whether your inventory, provider roadmap, cover holds and cross-border checks will catch a revoked identifier before a customer does, and whether you will be ready when Transport Canada finally publishes the transition clock for 1.3.1.


## FAQ


### Is CCMTA ELD Technical Standard 1.3.1 in force in Canada yet?


No. Transport Canada made version 1.3.1 public on July 29, 2026, and says it will lead implementation and coming into force with a transition for providers and certification bodies. As of early November 2026, no effective date has been published.


### When did Canada's federal ELD mandate start?


Federally regulated commercial drivers were required to use ELDs to complete records of duty status by June 12, 2021, with devices that meet the Hours of Service Regulations, the ELD Technical Standard and Transport Canada's certified list.


### Who is responsible if a device falls off Transport Canada's certified list?


The motor carrier is responsible for ensuring devices used by its drivers remain certified and listed. Buying a certified device once is not enough; status can change after installation.


### What happened with identifier DT4000 on October 13, 2026?


Transport Canada's certified ELD list shows identifier DT4000 (certification number 6T16) revoked on October 13, 2026. Carriers still using that identifier for federally regulated Canadian work should treat it as no longer certified and move to a listed device.


### Do U.S.-registered ELDs automatically qualify in Canada?


No. After June 12, 2021, U.S.-based carriers and drivers operating under Canada's federal rules need devices certified for Canada by a Transport Canada-accredited certification body. FMCSA registration alone is not sufficient.


### Should brokers verify Canadian ELD identifiers before covering a truck?


Yes. Require the Canadian ELD identifier and certification number, match both to Transport Canada's current list, and hold cover when the device is revoked or unverified, especially on cross-border and extra-provincial loads.
